name: Anekatangapadeswarar Temple, Kanchipuram
deity: Shiva as Anekatangapadeswarar (Anegabeswarar), worshipped with the goddess Kamakshi in the Kanchipuram tradition
period: Ancient Shiva shrine of Kanchipuram sung in the Tevaram (8th century); structural temple with later additions
summary: Anekatangapadeswarar, the Tiru Anekatangavadam of the Tevaram, is one of the ancient Shiva shrines of Kanchipuram, its legend tied above all to Ganesha, who is said to have set up the linga and worshipped the Lord here.

sections.history: Among the Paadal Petra shrines of Kanchipuram stands the temple of Anekatangapadeswarar, sung in the Tevaram, where the place is named Tiru Anekatangavadam. By tradition the linga was established by Vinayaka — Ganesha, the son of Shiva — who worshipped the Lord here, and the shrine is linked as well to Kubera, the lord of wealth, counted among its devotees. The temple stands within the old city among its many sanctuaries, built in the Dravidian manner and kept in worship to the present day under the state endowments board.
sections.architecture: The temple is built in the Dravidian style, its shrines set within a walled enclosure. It is entered from the north through a modest gopuram and from the east, where the Nandi and the balipeetha stand aligned with the gateway. The outer walls of the sanctum carry the attendant forms of a Shiva temple — Dakshinamurti, Vinayaka, Brahma, and the goddess Durga among them — set in their niches as the tradition prescribes. Following the Kanchipuram tradition, the Mother Goddess is worshipped as Kamakshi.
sections.legends: The legends of the shrine gather around Ganesha. By one account Vinayaka himself set up the linga here and worshipped it, and the name of the place is linked to the elephant, in keeping with his form. Tradition adds that the Lord of this shrine overcame a demon and arranged the marriage of a maiden, Vallabhai, to Vinayaka, and that Kubera, the keeper of wealth, counted himself among those who worshipped here. The stories differ in their detail from source to source, but hold in common the nearness of Ganesha to this sanctuary.
sections.festivals: The temple keeps a small number of festivals through the year, among them Karthikai in November or December, when lamps are lit in the Shaiva manner, and Maha Shivaratri in February or March. The monthly Pradosham is observed as at every Shiva temple, and the dates, following the Tamil calendar, are best confirmed locally.
sections.experience: Anekatangapadeswarar is a quiet shrine within the dense weave of Kanchipuram's temples, and a visit rewards the pilgrim who seeks out the city's Paadal Petra sites one by one. Come before the linga said to have been set up by Ganesha, walk the enclosure to see the sculpted forms in their niches, and take the shrine as one station in a longer round of Kanchi.

visit.timings: Typically open for limited hours in the morning and again in the evening, with a long midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands within Kanchipuram, about 75 km from Chennai and well connected by rail and road; Chennai holds the nearest international airport. Local buses and autos reach the temple's quarter. As several Kanchipuram shrines carry similar names, ask locally for the Anekatangavadam temple.
